newsitem.title: Germany: Industry sees Germany hitting EMU deficit goal.
newsitem.headline: Industry sees Germany hitting EMU deficit goal.

text.p: Leaders of Germany's powerful industry lobby said on Wednesday they were confident Bonn would be able to contain state borrowing enough this year to ensure the punctual start of European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the Federation of German Industry (BDI), said Germany would be able to keep its 1997 budget deficit below 3.0 percent of economic output, in line with borrowing guidelines set by the Maastricht Treaty.
Asked by a radio interviewer whether he shared the government's assurance that it could hold the deficit to its forecast 2.9 percent, Henkel said "I have no reason not to."
He added the deficit forecast was "a bit of a close shave" and Germany's economic performance was unconvincing. "But there are still opportunities for the government to do something," he said.
Hans-Peter Stihl, head of the Federation of German Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT), shared Henkel's view that Bonn would be able to control deficit spending.
"I am of the firm conviction that Germany and France will fulfill the strict EMU entry criteria," Stihl told reporters after being elected for a new term as DIHT president.

State secretary for finance Juergen Stark has this week defended the 2.9-percent deficit projection, saying it accounted for all recognisable risks and was not threatened even by a sharp jump in January unemployment to a 60-year record.
The Finance Ministry dismissed a German newspaper report on Wednesday the deficit would swell to 3.5 percent of GDP this year, reaffirming the figure stated by Stark.
The government is also discussing more austerity measures, but it must take care to cut consumption without trimming investment, Henkel said.

Stihl said he saw "big potential" for further government savings and opposed any possible increases in indirect taxes to plug budget gaps. He repeated calls for cuts in taxes and labour overheads to boost investment and job creation.
Henkel said Bonn's planned tax reform could also have a positive symbolic effect and greater flexibility on the labour market would help. The weaker mark would also give exporters a boost.
He conceded not all economic risks could be recognised as the past two years show. But he said the government had a realistic view of the labour market.
He also said he favoured a strict interpretation of the criteria for political, rather than economic, reasons.

"Many (German) politicians have been hectoring our partners for years about strict adherence to the convergence criteria," he said. "So we are now in the weakest position to say ... we can afford to be lax."
He noted that countries like Britain and the U.S. that have had the greatest success in bolstering their jobs markets in recent years have had stringent economic policies.
Portugal is likely to meet the EMU criteria, while Spain and Italy have shown great progress
"One thing we should keep in mind: currency union is coming. The parliaments have decided, entire nations have been polled, constitutions have been changed. Of that, there is no doubt," he said.
Henkel said he also shared the government view that countries' progress in meeting the convergence criteria should determine the start date for EMU, and not the other way around.
